summary: This PRB policy brief by Liz Creel, dated September 25, 2003, examines how population growth, migration, urbanization and economic activity degrade coastal regions, which hold about half the world's population. It covers the benefits and threats of coastal ecosystems, the effects of tourism, fishing and aquaculture, and health and gender impacts. It concludes with integrated coastal management and steps policymakers can take to include population data and gender dynamics in planning.
one_line: A 2003 PRB policy brief on how population growth, urbanization and economic activity threaten coastal ecosystems, and how integrated coastal management can respond.
key_facts: Approximately 3 billion people, about half of the world's population, live within 200 kilometers of a coastline, and by 2025 that figure is likely to double.
The average population density in coastal areas is about 80 persons per square kilometer, twice the world's average population density.
Along the Nile Delta, the population density reaches 500 to 1,000 people per square kilometer.
The population of Ecuador's Galapagos Islands has grown rapidly since the early 1980s, largely due to the arrival of coastal fishermen.
1,000 people arrive in China's large coastal cities each day.
In fact, 14 of the world's 17 largest cities are located along coasts, and eleven of these cities, including Bangkok, Jakarta, and Shanghai, are in Asia.
Mangroves line about 8 percent of the world's coastlines and 25 percent of the world's tropical coastlines.
Kenya, Liberia, the Philippines, and Puerto Rico have lost over 70 percent of their mangroves.
Tourism constitutes 95 percent of the economy of the Maldives and is the country's only source of hard currency.
In the Caribbean, official estimates say that 70,000 tons of waste are generated annually from tourism activities.
Marine fisheries and aquaculture produce close to 100 million tons of fish, shellfish, and edible plants every year, providing a livelihood for about 35 million people.
Eighty percent of marine pollution comes from land-based sources; the remaining 20 percent comes from atmospheric sources and marine-based sources such as oil spills.
In developing countries, more than 90 percent of wastewater and 70 percent of industrial wastes are discharged in coastal waters without being treated.

The Municipal Corporation of Brihan Mumbai, with support from the World Bank, has started the $300 million Bombay Sewage Disposal Project to collect and dispose of 80 percent of the sewage currently flowing untreated into the sea.
Women who fish in El Salvador earn only 40 percent of what men earn for fishing, and in rural Honduras women earn about half of what men do.
At least 107 of the world's 134 coastal developing nations are involved in some type of integrated coastal management effort at the national or subnational level.
